label: The Monge-Mather Shortening Principle
notes: This chapter, printed pages 163 through 204, asks why optimal trajectories cannot meet and then diverge. We introduce shortening as the geometric engine: any near-crossing of minimizers could be reconnected into a strictly cheaper configuration, which optimality forbids. Keep that single move in mind across every slide.

label: Action-Minimizing Curves
notes: Recall that displacement interpolation moves mass along minimizing geodesics, and Mather theory studies action-minimizing curves of a Lagrangian. Both share one defining property: each curve realizes the infimum of an action functional between its endpoints. That minimality is the only hypothesis the shortening argument will ever exploit.

label: The Crossing Configuration
notes: Picture two minimizers whose interiors pass very close to one another at nearby times. We label their endpoints and ask whether this can happen for genuine minimizers. The shortening principle answers no, but first we must make the dangerous configuration precise so the reconnection move has something to act on.

label: The Reconnection Move
notes: Here is the heart of the chapter. Swap the tails of two near-crossing curves at the meeting point, then smooth the corner. Triangle-type inequalities for the action say the rewired pair is strictly cheaper. Because the originals were minimizers, this contradiction shows near-crossings are impossible.

label: Why the Corner Saves Cost
notes: The cost saving comes from strict convexity of the Lagrangian in velocity. Cutting a corner shortens action; the gain is quadratic in the crossing gap while the smoothing penalty is higher order. We quantify the saving so the argument becomes an estimate, not merely a picture.

label: The Shortening Estimate
notes: The qualitative no-crossing statement upgrades to a quantitative bound: if two minimizers are close at two times, the whole pair stays uniformly close. This Monge-Mather estimate controls how far trajectories can drift, and it is the precise inequality that all later regularity results invoke.

label: No Crossing and Bounded Angle
notes: The estimate forbids transversal crossings of transport rays and bounds the angle at which nearby rays may meet. Two distinct minimizers cannot share an interior point, and rays fanning out of a region keep an ordered, non-tangling structure. This is the geometric payoff of the shortening move.

label: Intermediate-Time Regularity
notes: A striking consequence: even when endpoint transport maps are badly behaved, the interpolation at any interior time is far more regular. Mass occupying a midpoint comes from a single incoming and single outgoing direction, so the intermediate map is essentially Lipschitz. Shortening is what buys this smoothing.

label: Mather's Lagrangian Picture
notes: We connect to Mather theory in dynamics. Minimizing measures are invariant measures supported on action-minimizing orbits, and the Mather set has a graph property: over each base point sits a single velocity. Shortening is the transport-side reincarnation of exactly that graph property for Lagrangian flows.

label: From Estimate to Lipschitz Maps
notes: We assemble the pieces. The shortening estimate gives a modulus of continuity for the intermediate map, which becomes a genuine Lipschitz bound under mild cost regularity. This is the technical engine behind regularity of displacement interpolation and the absolute continuity of intermediate measures.

label: A Numerical Footprint
notes: The notebook makes the principle negotiable: a discrete transport plan with a before-and-after crossing diagram, and a recorded invariant that the shortened pairing has action no larger than the crossing pairing. Encourage students to move the crossing point and watch the saving shrink to zero exactly when the configuration stops being a real crossing.

label: Synthesis
notes: We close by tracing one idea through the chapter: minimality forbids near-crossings because reconnection would be cheaper, this yields a uniform estimate, the estimate forbids crossings and bounds angles, and that structure delivers intermediate-time regularity. The same logic links optimal transport to Mather's minimizing measures.
